questions.q: In a standard residential single-phase electrical system, how many wires are typically used to provide power and safety?
questions.n: This is the standard configuration for modern single-phase residential service, ensuring both functionality and safety.

questions.q: A three-phase, 4-wire (Wye) system is common in commercial buildings. What does the fourth wire represent?
questions.n: In a 3-phase Wye configuration, the fourth wire is the neutral, allowing for both phase-to-phase and phase-to-neutral voltages.

questions.q: According to the Philippine Electrical Code (PEC), what is the minimum wire size for a standard 20-Ampere convenience outlet branch circuit?
questions.n: This is the standard minimum size for 20-Ampere branch circuits to prevent overheating and voltage drop.

o: The maximum current a conductor can carry continuously without exceeding its temperature rating
The total resistance of the wire
questions.n: Ampacity is the 'Ampere Capacity' of a wire, determined by its size and insulation type.

questions.q: What color is standard for the 'Grounding Conductor' (Ground wire) in most electrical installations?
questions.n: Green, Green with Yellow stripes, or uninsulated copper are the universal indicators for ground.

questions.q: Why is it necessary to increase wire size (e.g., from No. 12 to No. 10) for very long runs of the same load?
o: To make the wire stronger physically
To allow for more wall outlets
To increase the speed of electricity
questions.n: Longer wires have more resistance; larger diameters reduce that resistance to keep voltage levels stable at the end of the line.

questions.q: In a 3-phase 'Delta' connection, how many wires are typically used for the power supply (excluding the ground)?
questions.n: A Delta connection uses three hot wires to create a triangle-like circuit, typically without a neutral.

questions.q: What is the primary function of a Circuit Breaker?
o: To protect the wire from overcurrent and short circuits
questions.n: Breakers 'trip' to cut off power when current exceeds safe limits, preventing fires.

questions.q: In a 3-phase, 3-wire Delta system, what is the standard voltage relationship between any two hot wires?
questions.n: Delta systems are primarily used for power loads where all three wires are 'hot' and the voltage is measured between them.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of quarter bends (90 degrees) allowed between pull points in a single conduit run according to the PEC?
questions.n: The code limits the total equivalent bends to 360 degrees to prevent excessive friction and wire damage during installation.

questions.q: When calculating the load for a branch circuit, what unit is typically used to represent the apparent power?
questions.n: Apparent power is the product of voltage and current without considering the power factor, expressed in VA.

questions.q: What is the minimum size of a copper equipment grounding conductor for a circuit protected by a 30-Ampere fuse or breaker?
questions.n: The grounding conductor must be sized based on the rating of the overcurrent device; 30A requires a No. 10 AWG.

questions.q: Which type of conduit is best suited for burial underground due to its corrosion resistance?
questions.n: PVC is the industry standard for underground use because it does not rust or corrode in damp soil.

questions.q: What is the demand factor for the first 3,000 VA of a general lighting load in a dwelling unit?
questions.n: The PEC requires the first 3,000 VA of a dwelling's lighting load to be calculated at full value.

questions.q: Which device is designed to protect people from electric shock by detecting small amounts of current leakage to ground?
questions.n: GFCIs monitor the balance of current between hot and neutral and trip if a tiny leakage (miliamps) occurs.

questions.q: What is the standard height for a wall-mounted convenience outlet from the finished floor line (FFL) in a standard residential design?
questions.n: 300 mm (roughly 12 inches) is the industry standard height for general-purpose wall outlets.

questions.q: How many 180 VA convenience outlets can be installed on a 20-Ampere branch circuit at 230V?
questions.n: Based on the 180 VA per outlet rule, a 20A circuit at 230V can support up to 25 outlets.

questions.q: Which of the following is the symbol for a 'Duplex Convenience Outlet, Grounding Type' on an electrical plan?
o: A circle with two parallel lines through it
A circle with a single line through it
questions.n: The two lines represent the 'duplex' nature of the outlet (two plug-in spots).

questions.q: What happens to the total resistance in a circuit when you add more loads in a 'Parallel' configuration?
questions.n: In a parallel circuit, the total resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance because more paths are provided.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a 'Service Entrance' in an architectural electrical design?
o: The point where the utility company's wires connect to the building's wiring
A place for building security to monitor electricity
questions.n: This is the gateway for power to enter the structure and connect to the main panelboard.

questions.q: Which electrical calculation is used to determine the appropriate size of a feeder conductor?
questions.n: Feeder sizing requires a comprehensive load schedule to determine the total demand on the system.

questions.q: What is the PEC required minimum clearance for electrical service drop conductors over a residential driveway?
questions.n: The PEC requires a minimum of 3.7 meters (12 feet) over residential driveways to ensure vehicle safety.

questions.q: What does a 'Transfer Switch' do in an electrical system with a generator?
o: It increases the voltage of the generator
It switches the power source between the utility grid and the generator
It measures how much power the generator is producing
questions.n: This prevents 'backfeeding' power into the grid, which is dangerous for utility workers.

questions.q: Which unit is used to measure the intensity of light falling on a surface, often used in architectural lighting requirements?
questions.n: Lux measures illuminance, which is the amount of light per unit area on a surface.

questions.q: In electrical wiring, what is 'Busbar'?
o: A tool used to bend conduit
The insulation around a large wire
A thick strip of copper or aluminum that conducts electricity within a switchboard or panelboard
questions.n: Busbars distribute high-current power to multiple circuit breakers or fuses.

questions.q: What is the 'Power Factor' (PF) in an AC circuit?
o: The speed at which the meter turns
The ratio of real power to apparent power
The total amount of voltage in the circuit
The number of phases in the system
questions.n: PF is the measurement of how effectively electrical power is being converted into useful work output.

questions.q: Which material has the highest electrical conductivity but is rarely used in standard building wiring due to cost?
questions.n: Silver is the most conductive metal known, but its extreme cost makes it impractical for general wiring.

questions.q: What is the maximum occupancy or floor area that requires a secondary emergency lighting system in commercial buildings?
o: Buildings with an occupant load of 50 or more
questions.n: Most safety codes require emergency lighting for assembly areas or places where many people congregate.

questions.q: Which type of transformer is used to lower the voltage from the utility street lines (e.g., 13.2kV) to building levels (e.g., 230V)?
questions.n: These transformers reduce high transmission voltages to lower, safer levels for end-use.

questions.q: What is the PEC standard for the color of the 'Neutral' wire?
questions.n: White is the most common, but gray is also an approved color for the neutral conductor.

questions.q: What is a 'Junction Box' used for in architectural wiring?
o: An enclosure where electrical wires are joined or connected
To act as a light fixture
questions.n: Junction boxes protect wire splices and provide accessibility for future maintenance.

questions.q: What does 'Short Circuit' mean?
o: A circuit used for low-voltage lighting
A circuit that has been turned off
A circuit that is not very long
An accidental low-resistance connection between two conductors
questions.n: This causes a massive surge of current which can trip breakers or cause fires.

questions.q: Which type of switch allows you to control a single light from two different locations?
questions.n: Two three-way switches are used in pairs to control a fixture from two points (e.g., top and bottom of stairs).

questions.q: What is the purpose of 'Direct Burial' cable (Type UF)?
o: Cable designed to be buried directly in the earth without conduit
questions.n: Type UF (Underground Feeder) has a tough, moisture-resistant jacket for soil contact.

questions.q: What is the standard unit of frequency for AC power in the Philippines?
questions.n: The Philippines follows the 60 Hz standard for alternating current, similar to North America.

questions.q: Which electrical component is used to store an electric charge and is often found in AC motor starters?
questions.n: Capacitors store energy in an electric field and help start motors or improve power factor.

questions.q: What is the load value used for a 'spare' branch circuit in a residential load calculation?
questions.n: 1,500 VA is the standard allowance for a spare circuit or small appliance circuit in many calculations.

questions.q: What does 'THHN' stand for on a wire jacket?
questions.n: This describes the material properties and the protective outer jacket of the conductor.

questions.q: In a lighting plan, what does a 'curved dashed line' between a switch and a light fixture represent?
o: The switch leg (the wiring connection that controls the light)
The physical conduit buried in the wall
questions.n: It indicates which switch operates which specific light fixture.

questions.q: Which type of light bulb is the most energy-efficient for modern architectural design?
questions.n: LEDs provide the most light per watt and have the longest lifespan.

questions.q: What is the PEC rule regarding the 'color' of the grounding conductor if it is insulated?
o: It can be any color as long as it's labeled
It must be green or green with a yellow stripe
questions.n: These are the globally recognized colors for safety grounding wires.

questions.q: What is the 'Utility Meter' used for?
o: To limit the amount of electricity a building can use
To measure the total energy consumption in kilowatt-hours (kWh)
questions.n: This information is used by the utility company for billing purposes.

questions.q: What is the standard 'clear working space' depth required in front of an electrical panelboard?
questions.n: The PEC requires a minimum of 900 mm of clear space in front of electrical equipment for safety.

questions.q: What does 'VA' stand for in electrical terms?
questions.n: VA is the unit for apparent power, calculated by multiplying voltage by current.

questions.q: In a residence, a 'Small Appliance Branch Circuit' is intended for which area?
questions.n: These circuits are specifically required to handle high-draw appliances like toasters and mixers.

questions.q: What is a 'Single-Line Diagram' in an electrical plan?
o: A floor plan with one wire drawn on it
A simplified schematic of the entire electrical distribution system
A list of all the light bulbs used
A drawing showing only one room
questions.n: It uses single lines and symbols to show how power flows from the service entrance to the loads.

questions.q: Which factor determines the 'Voltage Drop' in a wire?
o: Wire length, material, and cross-sectional area
questions.n: Longer, thinner wires have more resistance, leading to a greater loss of voltage.

questions.q: What is the main reason for 'Balancing' loads in a 3-phase system?
o: To prevent the lights from flickering
To save money on light switches
To minimize the current flowing through the neutral wire
questions.n: Balanced phases cancel each other out on the neutral; unbalanced loads create heat and waste energy.

questions.q: What is the maximum distance allowed between supports for a horizontal run of EMT conduit according to the PEC?
questions.n: The PEC generally requires EMT to be supported at least every 3 meters and within 0.9 meters of every box.

questions.q: Which of these is a 'Load-Bearing' electrical component?
questions.n: A motor is a load because it consumes energy to perform work (turning a fan, pump, etc.).

questions.q: In a multi-storey building, what is the 'Riser'?
o: A tool used to lift heavy panels
The top of a stair step
The vertical portion of the electrical distribution system
questions.n: The riser consists of the conduits and cables that carry power vertically between floors.

questions.q: What is 'Diversity Factor' in electrical load calculation?
o: The number of different types of wires used
The difference between AC and DC power
The efficiency of a light bulb
The ratio of the sum of individual maximum demands to the maximum demand of the whole system
questions.n: It accounts for the fact that not all appliances/loads in a building will be 'on' at the same time.

questions.q: What does a 'Main Lug Only' (MLO) panelboard lack?
questions.n: An MLO panel is fed directly from another panel and doesn't have its own main disconnect switch.

questions.q: Which of these devices is used to protect against overvoltage caused by lightning?
questions.n: Surge arresters divert high-voltage spikes from lightning or power surges safely into the ground.

questions.q: What is the maximum voltage drop allowed for a branch circuit according to most design standards (including the PEC)?
questions.n: A 3% drop for branch circuits is the standard limit to ensure equipment runs efficiently.

questions.q: Why are electrical panelboards usually located in accessible areas like hallways or utility rooms?
o: To show them off as a design feature
To allow for quick emergency shutoff and maintenance
To keep them away from children
questions.n: In case of fire or shock, you need to be able to reach the breakers quickly without moving furniture.
